page_header: Principles of Inheritance and Variation (Botany-II) · 4 marks

steps.label: Definition
steps.margin_note: Definition plus one line on why the recessive parent. Five lines.
lines: A TEST CROSS is a cross between an individual
showing the DOMINANT character and the
HOMOZYGOUS RECESSIVE parent.
The recessive parent is always used, because it
contributes only recessive alleles.
steps.why: A homozygous recessive parent can only give recessive gametes, so anything dominant that appears in the progeny must have come from the unknown parent.
common_mistakes: Crossing with a dominant parent. A test cross uses the HOMOZYGOUS RECESSIVE one.
Leaving out 'homozygous'. A heterozygous partner would not give a clean answer.
steps.memory_tip: Cross it with a plant that can hide nothing.

steps.label: What it is used for
steps.margin_note: Say what is unknown and why it cannot be seen.
lines: A test cross is used to find out whether an
individual showing the dominant character is
HOMOZYGOUS (TT) or HETEROZYGOUS (Tt).
Both look the same from outside, so the
genotype cannot be told by appearance.
steps.why: Two different genotypes can produce the same appearance, so the only way to tell them apart is to look at what they produce.
common_mistakes: Saying a test cross finds the phenotype. The phenotype is already visible; the cross finds the GENOTYPE.
Saying it works on recessive individuals. A recessive individual's genotype is already known — it must be tt.
steps.memory_tip: You can see the phenotype; the cross tells you the genotype.

steps.label: The design
steps.margin_note: Both cases with both ratios. This is the 'design' the question asks for.
lines: Unknown violet plant (W_)  ×  white (ww)
CASE 1 — if the unknown is HOMOZYGOUS (WW):
all offspring are Ww, all violet.
Ratio 1 : 0
CASE 2 — if the unknown is HETEROZYGOUS (Ww):
offspring are 1 Ww violet : 1 ww white.
Ratio 1 : 1
steps.why: The two cases give visibly different progeny, so a single cross settles the question by inspection.
common_mistakes: Giving only one case. The test works because the TWO cases differ.
Saying case 1 gives 3:1. A homozygous dominant parent gives ALL dominant offspring.
steps.memory_tip: All dominant means homozygous; half recessive means heterozygous.

steps.label: The two ratios
steps.margin_note: Both ratios plus the reason they are equal. That last line is worth writing.
lines: A MONOHYBRID test cross of a heterozygote gives
a phenotypic ratio of 1 : 1.
A DIHYBRID test cross of a double heterozygote
In a test cross the phenotypic and genotypic
ratios are the SAME.
steps.why: Because the recessive parent adds nothing visible, every progeny class shows the gamete it received from the unknown parent — so the ratios cannot differ.
common_mistakes: Giving 3:1 for a monohybrid test cross. That is a SELFING ratio; a test cross gives 1:1.
Leaving out the dihybrid case. Both ratios are named in the book.
steps.memory_tip: Test cross ratios read the gametes directly, so both ratios match.

steps.label: Diagram — test cross
steps.margin_note: No diagram mark, but 'design a test cross' invites the drawing. The one-row square is the clearest thing you can put on the page.

elements.caption: Step 1 — the F₁ crossed with the recessive parent
Step 2 — the square: the recessive parent gives one gamete only
Step 3 — the progeny and the ratio

steps.why: The square has only one row because the recessive parent makes only one kind of gamete, and that single row is the whole reason a test cross works.
common_mistakes: Drawing a full 2 by 2 square. The recessive parent gives ONE gamete, so there is one row.
Giving the recessive parent two different gametes. ww makes only w.
Labelling the progeny with genotypes but no phenotypes. Both are read off this square.
steps.memory_tip: One row, because one parent has only one gamete to give.
